analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale and manufacture of gas-operated semi-automatic firearms and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced April 9, 2025 with 84 cosponsors — every one a Democrat — was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The GOSAFE Act would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, or transfer semi-automatic firearms that the Attorney General lists as prohibited gas-operated guns, along with parts kits to build them and devices that speed up their rate of fire. It would also ban the sale and manufacture of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Guns and magazines legally owned before the law would stay legal to keep, but owners could only transfer them to immediate family through a licensed dealer, and communities could use federal justice grants to pay people who surrender them.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by gun violence would benefit if the ban reduces access to the semi-automatic rifles and high-capacity magazines most often used in mass shootings, since new sales and manufacturing of covered guns would end. People who want to turn in covered firearms would be compensated under local buy-back programs funded through Byrne justice grants. Police, and federal, state, and tribal agencies keep full access to the banned firearms.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the import, sale, manufacture, transfer, receipt, and (for newly made guns) possession of semi-automatic firearms the Attorney General lists as prohibited gas-operated guns, plus the parts and devices used to build or modify them — a category aimed at the AR- and AK-pattern rifles used in many mass shootings.

Outlaws the sale and manufacture of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with possession banned only for devices made after enactment — so existing magazines stay with their current owners.
Adds a 2-to-10-year federal penalty (with a 2-year mandatory minimum) for anyone who commits another federal felony while possessing a prohibited firearm.
Lets state and local governments use Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to pay people who surrender covered firearms and magazines under buy-back programs.

Requires the ATF to publish a public list of prohibited models, lets the public sue if the Attorney General removes a firearm from that list, and routes application fees and existing federal firearms taxes into a Firearm Safety Trust Fund to pay for enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and magazine manufacturers lose a large civilian market and must pay fees and navigate an Attorney General approval process for any new semi-automatic design. Licensed dealers stop selling covered guns and magazines and must record each buyer's acknowledgment of the prohibited list. Current owners of covered firearms keep them but can no longer sell them or give them to anyone except immediate family through a licensed dealer, and violations carry fines of up to $5,000 and up to 12 months in prison. Enforcement is funded by fees and existing federal firearms taxes rather than new general spending.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and current owners

drawbacks.text: The banned category reaches well beyond 'military-style' rifles. The bill's definition of gas-operated includes blowback- and recoil-operated actions, and the exemptions cover bolt, lever, and pump actions, single-shots, and fixed magazines — so common semi-automatic hunting rifles with detachable magazines and some pistols could be prohibited unless redesigned.

Current owners of covered firearms keep them but lose the ability to sell or transfer them to anyone outside the immediate family, even through a licensed dealer, which reduces the resale value of legally purchased property.
Violations carry criminal penalties — up to a $5,000 fine and 12 months in prison for each offense — exposing otherwise law-abiding owners to prosecution over paperwork and transfer mistakes.

The grandfathering limits the near-term effect: millions of covered firearms and pre-enactment magazines would remain legally possessed, so the bill mostly restricts future supply rather than guns already in circulation, and its effect on gun violence is therefore uncertain and debated.

The new design-approval regime — detailed applications, physical samples, perjury attestation, fees, and up to 240 days for review — is a compliance burden that larger manufacturers are better positioned to absorb than small gun makers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the firearms and magazines most often used in mass shootings and gives the ATF a mechanism to keep new workarounds off the market, which supporters would call a real public-safety gain. The costs are also real: the ban's broad definitions would capture some ordinary hunting and target guns along with AR- and AK-pattern rifles, current owners lose the right to sell or transfer their property, and the grandfathered stock means the safety benefit builds only slowly over time. The design-approval process adds significant regulatory cost to the industry. On balance it is a genuine restriction on a widely held consumer product, pursued for public-safety reasons, whose effectiveness depends on contested assumptions about how much these specific weapons drive gun deaths.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote has happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the GOSAFE Act on April 9, 2025, with 25 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, which is the standard first step for gun legislation in the House.
Support grew to 84 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat; no Republican signed on.

The action history shows nothing after the referral — the bill has not been scheduled for a committee markup or a floor vote, and with a Republican House majority and no Republican support it has no active path forward.
Because this Congress runs through January 3, 2027, the bill technically remains alive and could still be taken up, but bills that sit in committee this long with no movement almost never advance.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, opponents of the ban. Current law stands unchanged: manufacturers continue to sell the semi-automatic rifles and large-capacity magazines the bill would prohibit, and current owners face no new restrictions. Supporters of the ban have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and current owners, so far

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the GOSAFE Act and recruited 25 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: 84 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill its full House support base; every cosponsor is a Democrat.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Gun rights advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Oppose bans on semi-automatic rifles and large-capacity magazines and pressure lawmakers against them; such groups are the primary outside opposition to this type of bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is entirely Democratic: all 84 cosponsors are Democrats, no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee has not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill ends civilian manufacture and sale of the most popular semi-automatic rifle category and any other gun the Attorney General lists, and requires Attorney General approval — with fees — for new semi-automatic designs. The industry's interest in preserving that market runs directly against the bill's stated public-safety goal, though the approval regime's cost falls harder on small makers than large ones.
Sale and manufacture of any feeding device holding more than 10 rounds would be banned outright, eliminating a product line that attaches to most modern semi-automatic rifles and pistols.

Dealers would lose sales of covered firearms and magazines and would have to record each buyer's acknowledgment of the prohibited list before selling any semi-automatic firearm, adding compliance work to remaining sales.

analysis.trajectory: Realistically the bill dies in committee. It has no Republican cosponsors, the House and Senate are both run by Republicans, and seven months after introduction there is no hearing or markup. Its most likely end is expiring quietly when this Congress adjourns in January 2027, as previous assault-weapon and magazine ban bills have; it could be reintroduced if Democrats win the majority in the 2026 midterms.
